analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income and corporate taxes with a simpler graduated tax and a business profits tax, and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: Introduced on October 5, 1998 with zero cosponsors, the bill never left the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the current federal income tax on individuals and corporations and replace it with a two-part system: a simple graduated tax on individuals at 15, 25, and 30 percent, and a tax on business gross profits at 8 and 12 percent. Workers would get their Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes credited against, and refunded from, their income tax, and families would get allowances and deductions for living costs, education, mortgage interest, and charitable giving. It would also repeal the estate and gift tax, keep 401(k) and Roth IRA savings tax-free, and place an 11 percent tax on imports while leaving exports untaxed.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers would see the biggest direct gain: the bill makes the employee share of payroll taxes a refundable credit, so a worker whose income tax bill is smaller than their payroll tax would get the difference back as a refund. Families would benefit from a 'family living allowance' that exempts the first dollars earned, a deduction of up to $4,000 per student for college tuition, the mortgage interest deduction, and a much shorter tax form. Heirs to large estates would gain from full repeal of the estate and gift tax, and households able to save would gain from unlimited Roth IRA contributions.

how_it_helps.text: The employee's share of Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes would be credited against the new individual income tax and refunded if it exceeds tax owed, without reducing Social Security trust funds or benefits.
A 'family living allowance' ($8,140 for a married couple) would exempt the first dollars a family earns from tax, alongside personal exemptions of $2,700 each.
Families could deduct up to $4,000 of college tuition and fees per student (capped at $12,000 per return), plus mortgage interest on up to $1 million of home debt and charitable contributions.
The bill would keep 401(k) plans and deductible IRAs intact and let anyone contribute up to their full income to a tax-free Roth IRA with no required withdrawals during life.
Individual rates would be graduated at 15, 25, and 30 percent, and the bill claims the tax return would be 'only a small fraction the size of Form 1040.'
U.S.-made exports would leave the country free of the business tax, which the bill frames as helping American firms compete internationally.

analysis.who_pays: Workers whose health, life, or disability insurance is paid by an employer would pay tax on that coverage as income, a real cost for millions of people with employer health plans. Consumers would likely bear much of the new 11 percent import tax through higher prices on imported goods. The Treasury would lose the estate and gift tax, shifting the cost of financing the payroll-tax refunds and rate structure onto other taxes. Businesses would pay a new 8 to 12 percent tax on gross profits, though they would get credit for the employer share of payroll taxes they pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers with employer coverage, import buyers

drawbacks.text: Full repeal of the estate and gift tax would eliminate a tax paid almost entirely by the largest estates, a large cut concentrated at the top of the wealth distribution.
Employer-paid health, life, and disability insurance and other fringe benefits would become taxable income for employees, raising tax bills for many workers who currently receive coverage tax-free.
The bill imposes an import tax of 11 percent of customs value, which importers would likely pass along to consumers as higher prices on imported goods.
Allowing unlimited Roth IRA contributions up to a person's full adjusted gross income primarily helps households with enough surplus income to save large sums.

The business tax and import tax were untested, and outside analysts had long debated whether a border-adjusted tax shifts its real burden onto consumers, so the distributional claims in the findings were contestable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuinely two-sided proposal. The refundable payroll tax credit is a large, concrete gain for low-income workers, and the simplification, education deduction, and family allowance would help many ordinary households. Against that, estate tax repeal hands a large cut to the wealthiest families, taxing employer health coverage raises costs on a middle-class benefit, and the import tax would raise consumer prices. Whether the whole package raised or lowered any given family's taxes depended on their income, savings, and benefits, and the bill never received the analysis or debate that would have settled it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on introduction, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil English (R-PA) introduced the Simplified USA Tax Act of 1998 on October 5, 1998, with introductory remarks on October 2.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, and no further action was ever taken on it.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill died in committee when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without ever receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

The bill was a later version of the 'USA Tax' concept English had previously proposed: a graduated individual tax with a refundable payroll tax credit, a business tax on gross profits with border adjustments, and repeal of the estate and gift tax.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one's taxes changed. The beneficiaries were the status quo itself: the existing tax code, with all of its current rates, deductions, and the estate tax, remained in place, and no industry or household gained or lost anything from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one — the tax code stayed the same

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 5, 1998 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor two days earlier; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on October 5, 1998 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the bill never revealed whether support or opposition split by party; it was carried entirely by one Republican sponsor.

industries.note: Full repeal of the estate and gift tax would eliminate a levy borne almost entirely by the largest estates, with the lost revenue made up elsewhere in the tax system.

Unlimited Roth IRA contributions up to full income, no required distributions before death, and continued 401(k) deferrals would channel more household savings into managed accounts. Ordinary retirement savers would benefit too, but households able to save large amounts would capture most of the tax advantage.
Exports would leave the country free of the business tax, lowering the tax burden on U.S.-made goods sold abroad; American factory jobs and export firms would be the intended winners.
An 11 percent tax on the customs value of imported goods and services would raise their costs, most of which would likely be passed to consumers as higher prices.
A code with few deductions and a return described as a small fraction the size of Form 1040 would sharply shrink the market for tax preparation and compliance services.

Businesses would pay a new 8 to 12 percent tax on gross profits, but they would receive a credit for the employer share of Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes they pay, reducing that labor cost.
